questions.explanation: 'Have to' expresses obligation. With you, use 'have'.

wrongReasons.has: 'has' is used with he, she and it.

questions.text: You ___ to wear a uniform at this school. It's a rule.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb talks about past habits that have finished.

wrongReasons.at: 'used at' is not a correct structure here.

questions.text: I used ___ play football when I was young.

questions.explanation: In present perfect questions about life experience, use 'ever' before the participle: Have you ever been to Rome?

wrongReasons.never: 'never' is negative; in questions we use 'ever'.
wrongReasons.yet: 'yet' usually goes at the end of the question.

questions.text: Have you ___ tried Indian food in your life? – No, never.

questions.explanation: Use 'since' with a point in time: I have lived here since 2015.

wrongReasons.for: 'for' is used with a period of time (for five years), not a starting point.
wrongReasons.from: 'from' needs 'to/until'; with the present perfect and a starting point, use 'since'.

questions.text: She has worked at the hospital ___ 2019.

questions.explanation: Use 'for' with a period of time: She has been here for two hours.

wrongReasons.since: 'since' is used with a point in time (since 2018), not a period.
wrongReasons.during: 'during' is not used with the present perfect to say how long.

questions.text: We have lived in this flat ___ six years.

questions.explanation: Use 'yet' at the end of negative sentences in the present perfect: I haven't eaten yet.

wrongReasons.already: 'already' is used in positive sentences, not with 'haven't'.
wrongReasons.still: 'still' goes before the verb: I still haven't finished.

questions.text: I can't go out now. I haven't finished my homework ___.

questions.explanation: Use 'already' (or 'just') between 'has/have' and the participle: She has already left.

wrongReasons.yet: 'yet' is used in questions and negatives, not in positive sentences.
wrongReasons.ever: 'ever' is used in questions about experience, not here.

questions.text: Don't worry about the tickets. Tom has ___ bought them.

questions.explanation: The present perfect is have/has + past participle. With plural subjects use 'have': They have never met.

wrongReasons.has: 'has' is for he, she and it; 'my parents' is plural.
wrongReasons.did: 'visited' after 'did' is wrong; 'did' needs the base form.

questions.text: My parents ___ never visited Scotland.

questions.explanation: Present perfect = has/have + past participle. 'Win' is irregular: win – won – won.

wrongReasons.win: After 'has' we need the past participle, not the base form.
wrongReasons.winned: 'win' is irregular: the past participle is 'won'.

questions.text: Our team has ___ the match! We're the champions!

questions.explanation: Use 'How long have you + past participle' for a situation that continues now: How long have you lived here?

wrongReasons.do: 'known' is a past participle, so it needs 'have', not 'do'.
wrongReasons.did: 'did' is followed by the base form 'know', not 'known'.

questions.text: How long ___ you known your best friend?

questions.explanation: After a superlative, use the present perfect with 'ever': It's the best book I have ever read.

wrongReasons.saw: 'saw' is the past simple; after 'have' we need the participle 'seen'.
wrongReasons.see: After 'have' we need the past participle, not the base form.

questions.text: This is the best film I have ever ___.

questions.explanation: Use has/have + just + participle for something that happened a moment ago: She has just arrived.

wrongReasons.have: 'have' is for I, you, we and they; with 'he' use 'has'.
wrongReasons.is: 'is' + 'left' is not the present perfect; use 'has'.

questions.text: He ___ just left the office, so you can't speak to him now.

questions.explanation: Use 'since' with a point in time: I've been ill since Friday.

wrongReasons.for: 'for' needs a length of time; 'last Monday' is a point in time.
wrongReasons.ago: 'ago' goes after a time period and is used with the past simple.

questions.text: I've known about the problem ___ last Monday.

questions.explanation: Use 'for' with a period of time: We haven't met for years.

wrongReasons.since: 'since' is followed by a point in time, not 'a long time'.
wrongReasons.during: 'during' does not say how long something has continued.

questions.text: They haven't spoken to each other ___ a long time.

questions.explanation: Use 'yet' at the end of present perfect questions: Have you finished yet?

wrongReasons.still: 'still' does not go at the end of a question like this.
wrongReasons.since: 'since' needs a point in time after it.

questions.text: Has the parcel arrived ___? I'm still waiting for it.

questions.explanation: After 'It's the first time', use the present perfect: It's the first time I have flown.

wrongReasons.rode: 'rode' is the past simple; after 'have' use 'ridden'.
wrongReasons.ride: After 'have' we need the past participle, not the base form.

questions.text: It's the first time I have ___ a horse.

questions.explanation: 'Has gone to' means the person is there now or on the way: He has gone to the bank.

wrongReasons.in: With 'go' we show movement, so use 'to', not 'in'.
wrongReasons.at: 'at' is not used after 'gone' for a city.

questions.text: My sister has gone ___ Paris, so she isn't at home.

questions.explanation: Use the present perfect for actions in a time period that is not finished (this week): I have called her twice today.
questions.text: The bus ___ been late three times this week.

questions.explanation: Present perfect with 'already': have/has + already + participle. We have already eaten.

wrongReasons.has: 'has' is for he, she and it; with 'we' use 'have'.
wrongReasons.did: 'did' is followed by the base form, and 'already' goes with the present perfect.

questions.text: We ___ already sent the invitations for the party.

questions.explanation: Use 'never' with the present perfect for no experience at any time: I've never seen snow.

wrongReasons.ever: 'ever' is not used in positive statements like this; use 'never'.
wrongReasons.already: 'already' does not fit with 'in my life' here.

questions.text: I've ___ been so tired in my life! I need a holiday.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous for a longer action and the past simple for the short action that interrupts it: I was reading when he called.

wrongReasons.ringed: 'ring' is irregular: the past simple is 'rang'.
wrongReasons.was ringing: The short action that interrupts uses the past simple, not the past continuous.

questions.text: I was cooking dinner when the phone ___.

questions.explanation: Past continuous = was/were + -ing. With 'we' use 'were': We were watching TV.

wrongReasons.was: 'was' is for I, he, she and it; with 'we' use 'were'.
wrongReasons.are: The story is in the past, so use 'were', not 'are'.

questions.text: While we ___ walking in the park, it started to rain.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a time in the past: What were you doing at 6 pm?

wrongReasons.do: After 'were you' we need the -ing form.

questions.text: What were you ___ at eight o'clock last night?

questions.explanation: Past continuous = was/were + -ing: He was sleeping when I arrived.

wrongReasons.were: 'were' is for you, we and they; with 'she' use 'was'.
wrongReasons.is: The sentence is about the past, so use 'was'.

questions.text: She ___ reading a book when the lights went out.

questions.explanation: Use 'when' before the short past simple action: I was working when she phoned.

wrongReasons.while: 'while' usually goes with the longer action; for the short action use 'when'.
wrongReasons.during: 'during' is followed by a noun, not a clause.

questions.text: The children were playing football ___ their mother called them in.

questions.explanation: Use 'while' or 'when' before the longer past continuous action: She fell while she was running.

wrongReasons.during: 'during' is followed by a noun (during the trip), not a subject and verb.
wrongReasons.since: 'since' does not mean 'at the same time as' here.

questions.text: I saw an accident ___ I was driving to work.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action in progress at a past time: At ten I was working.

wrongReasons.studied: 'were studied' is passive and does not fit here.

questions.text: At midnight they were still ___ for the exam.

questions.explanation: After 'while', use the past continuous for the longer action: She cut her finger while she was cooking.

wrongReasons.has: 'has skiing' is not correct; use 'was skiing'.

questions.text: He broke his leg while he ___ skiing in the mountains.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous for the background situation in the past: It was raining when I woke up.

wrongReasons.is: 'this morning' is finished and the sentence is in the past.

questions.text: It ___ snowing when we left the house this morning.

questions.explanation: Negative past continuous = wasn't/weren't + -ing: They weren't working.

wrongReasons.didn't: 'didn't' needs the base form, not the -ing form.

questions.text: We ___ listening, so we didn't hear what the teacher said.

questions.explanation: Past continuous (was/were + -ing) for the longer action, past simple for the sudden event: I was writing when the computer crashed.

wrongReasons.do: After 'were' we need the -ing form, not the base form.

questions.text: Two scientists were ___ an experiment when the machine suddenly stopped.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous for an action already in progress when something happened: When I got home, they were eating.
questions.text: When I arrived at the party, my friends ___ dancing.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous to explain what you were in the middle of: I was driving, so I couldn't answer.

wrongReasons.am: The call was in the past, so use 'was'.

questions.text: Sorry, I didn't answer your call. I ___ having a shower.

questions.explanation: Use the past continuous to describe a background scene in a story: The wind was blowing.

wrongReasons.are: The description is in the past, so use 'were'.

questions.text: The sun was shining and the birds ___ singing.

questions.explanation: Past continuous questions: was/were + subject + -ing: What were you doing at noon?
questions.text: What ___ you doing when the earthquake happened?

questions.explanation: The short action is in the past simple and the longer action in the past continuous: I lost my wallet while I was shopping.

wrongReasons.losed: 'lose' is irregular: the past simple is 'lost'.
wrongReasons.was losing: Losing keys is a short action, so use the past simple.

questions.text: I ___ my keys while I was running for the bus.

questions.explanation: Use 'during' + noun for a period of time: It was raining during the night.

wrongReasons.while: 'while' needs a subject and verb after it, not a noun.
wrongReasons.when: 'when' is followed by a clause, not just 'the war'.

questions.text: My grandfather was working in a factory ___ the war, while the soldiers were away fighting.

questions.explanation: Past continuous for the long action, past simple for the short one: He was talking when someone shouted.

wrongReasons.throwed: 'throw' is irregular: the past simple is 'threw'.
wrongReasons.was throwing: The sudden short action uses the past simple.

questions.text: The politician was giving a speech when someone ___ an egg at him.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional for facts: If + present, present. If you heat water, it boils.

wrongReasons.melted: This is a general fact, so we use the present, not the past.

questions.text: If you heat ice, it ___.

questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + verb. If it rains, I'll stay in.

wrongReasons.will rain: We don't use 'will' in the if-clause of a first conditional.

questions.text: If it ___ tomorrow, we will stay at home.

questions.explanation: In the first conditional, the if-clause uses the present simple: I'll tell you if I see him.

wrongReasons.will get: Don't use 'will' after 'if'; use the present simple.
wrongReasons.got: The news is in the future, so use the present simple, not the past.

questions.text: I'll call you if I ___ any news.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not': You'll be late unless you leave now.

wrongReasons.if: 'if you hurry' gives the opposite meaning; you need 'unless' (= if not).
wrongReasons.without: 'without' is followed by a noun or -ing form, not a clause.

questions.text: You will miss the train ___ you hurry.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional for things that are always true: If + present, present. If you don't eat, you get hungry.

wrongReasons.won't: This is a general fact (zero conditional), so we don't use 'won't' after 'if'.

questions.text: Plants die if they ___ get enough water.

questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + verb. If he wins, he'll be happy.
questions.text: If she ___ the exam, her parents will be very proud.

questions.explanation: In the if-clause of the first conditional, use the present simple, also in the negative: If I don't go, I'll call you.

wrongReasons.won't: Don't use 'won't' in the if-clause; use 'don't'.
wrongReasons.didn't: The situation is in the future, so use the present 'don't'.

questions.text: What will you do if you ___ find a job this summer?

questions.explanation: Zero conditional for facts: If you mix red and white, you get pink.

wrongReasons.got: This is a general fact, so use the present, not the past.

questions.text: If you mix blue and yellow, you ___ green.

questions.explanation: Use 'if' + present simple, then an imperative for advice or offers: If you are cold, close the window.

wrongReasons.unless: 'unless' means 'if not', which gives the wrong meaning.
wrongReasons.so: 'so' shows a result and cannot start this condition.

questions.text: ___ you need help with the project, just ask me.

questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + verb. If you are late, you will miss the start.

wrongReasons.be: With 'he' we need 'is', not the base form.

questions.text: If he ___ late again, the boss will be angry.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional with 'if' or 'when' for scientific facts: Ice melts when it gets warm.

wrongReasons.unless: 'unless' means 'if not', so the meaning is wrong.
wrongReasons.so: 'so' shows a result, but heating is the condition.

questions.text: Water boils ___ you heat it to 100 degrees Celsius.

questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + verb. If I see him, I'll tell him.

wrongReasons.will see: After 'if' we use the present simple, not 'will'.
wrongReasons.saw: The meeting is in the future, so use the present 'see'.

questions.text: If I ___ Maria at the meeting, I'll give her your message.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional for things that always happen: If you press it, it rings.

wrongReasons.will open: This is a general truth, so we don't use 'will' after 'if'.

questions.text: The alarm goes off if somebody ___ the door.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional: If + present, present. If you click here, the page opens.

wrongReasons.turn: 'the machine' is singular, so the verb needs -s.
wrongReasons.turned: This is a present or future result, not the past.

questions.text: If you press this button, the machine ___ off.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' = 'if not': I won't go unless you come with me.

wrongReasons.if: 'We won't go if the weather is good' does not make sense here; use 'unless'.
wrongReasons.when: 'when' gives the wrong meaning; you need 'unless' (= if not).

questions.text: We won't go to the beach ___ the weather is good.

questions.explanation: In the first conditional, use the present simple after 'if': If it's sunny, we'll go out.

wrongReasons.was: The sentence is about now and the future, so use 'is'.

questions.text: If the shop ___ closed, I'll buy the milk tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Zero conditional for habits and facts: If + present, present. My cat hides if it hears thunder.

wrongReasons.will come: This is a general habit, so don't use 'will' after 'if'.

questions.text: My dog barks if anybody ___ near the house.

questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + verb. If you study, you'll pass.

wrongReasons.will come: Don't use 'will' after 'if' in the first conditional.
wrongReasons.came: The party is in the future, so use the present simple.

questions.text: If you ___ to the party, you'll meet my cousin.

questions.explanation: Past simple passive = was/were + past participle: The house was built in 1950.

wrongReasons.is: 'in 1890' is in the past, so use 'was'.

questions.text: This bridge ___ built in 1890.

questions.explanation: Present simple passive = am/is/are + past participle: French is spoken in Canada.

wrongReasons.speak: The passive needs the past participle, not the base form.
wrongReasons.spoke: 'spoke' is the past simple; the participle is 'spoken'.

questions.text: English is ___ in many countries around the world.

questions.explanation: Past passive = was/were + past participle: The windows were broken yesterday.

wrongReasons.are: 'last night' is in the past, so use 'were'.

questions.text: The thieves ___ caught by the police last night.

questions.explanation: Use 'made from' when the material changes: Wine is made from grapes.

wrongReasons.of: 'made of' is for materials you can still see; wood changes into paper, so use 'from'.
wrongReasons.by: 'by' introduces who does the action, not the material.

questions.text: Paper is made ___ wood.

questions.explanation: In the passive, use 'by' for the person who does the action: The song was sung by a child.

wrongReasons.from: In the passive, the person who does the action comes after 'by'.

questions.text: The novel was written ___ a young teacher from Wales.

questions.explanation: Present passive = am/is/are + past participle: These shoes are made in Italy.

wrongReasons.have: 'have made' is active; the passive needs 'are/were made'.

questions.text: These cars ___ made in Germany. Look at the label.

questions.explanation: Use the present simple passive for regular actions: The rooms are cleaned every day.

wrongReasons.were: 'nowadays' talks about the present, so use 'are', not 'were'.

questions.text: Nowadays the windows ___ cleaned every Friday.

questions.explanation: Past passive questions: Was/Were + subject + past participle? Was the car repaired?

wrongReasons.send: The passive needs the past participle, not the base form.

questions.text: Was the letter ___ by post yesterday?

questions.explanation: Present passive = is/are + past participle: Rice is grown in Asia.

wrongReasons.grows: 'grows grown' is not possible; the passive is 'is grown'.

questions.text: Coffee ___ grown in Brazil and Colombia.

questions.explanation: Past passive = was/were + past participle + by: The school was opened by the mayor.

wrongReasons.open: After 'was' the passive needs the past participle.
wrongReasons.opening: 'was opening' is active and needs an object.

questions.text: The new hospital was officially ___ by the Prime Minister on Monday, and the first patients arrived the next day.

questions.explanation: Past passive = was/were + past participle: The roads were closed by the snow.

wrongReasons.are: 'last winter' is in the past, so use 'were'.

questions.text: Many trees ___ destroyed by the storm last winter.

questions.explanation: Past passive = was/were + past participle: The match was stopped because of the rain.

wrongReasons.cancel: After 'was' the passive needs the past participle.
wrongReasons.cancelling: 'was cancelling' is active; the flight did not cancel something.

questions.text: Our flight was ___ because of the snow.

questions.explanation: Negative present passive = am/is/are + not + past participle: Dogs are not allowed here.

wrongReasons.do: 'do not allowed' is wrong; the passive uses 'be'.

questions.text: Mobile phones ___ not allowed in the exam room.

questions.explanation: Use the past passive for finished past actions: This church was designed by a famous architect.

wrongReasons.is: The painting was made in the past, so use 'was'.
wrongReasons.were: 'the Mona Lisa' is singular, so use 'was'.

questions.text: The Mona Lisa ___ painted by Leonardo da Vinci.

questions.explanation: Past passive questions: Where/When + was/were + subject + past participle? When was the tower built?

wrongReasons.did: 'did ... held' is wrong; the passive question uses 'were'.

questions.text: Where ___ the first modern Olympic Games held?

questions.explanation: Present passive for routines: is/are + past participle. The post is delivered at nine.

wrongReasons.collect: After 'is' the passive needs the past participle.
wrongReasons.collecting: 'is collecting' is active; the rubbish does not collect anything.

questions.text: The rubbish is ___ every Tuesday morning.

questions.explanation: Past passive = was/were + past participle: He was sent home early.

wrongReasons.is: 'last month' is in the past, so use 'was'.

questions.text: The criminal ___ sent to prison for five years last month.

questions.explanation: Present passive = is/are + past participle: Lunch is served at one.

wrongReasons.serve: After 'is' the passive needs the past participle.
wrongReasons.serving: 'is serving' is active; breakfast does not serve anything.

questions.text: Breakfast is ___ from seven to ten in this hotel.

questions.explanation: Use 'mustn't' or 'can't' for things that are not allowed: You mustn't park here.

wrongReasons.don't have to: 'don't have to' means it is not necessary, but here it is forbidden.
wrongReasons.shouldn't: 'shouldn't' is only advice; the law forbids it, so use 'mustn't'.

questions.text: You ___ smoke in the hospital. It's against the law.

questions.explanation: 'Don't have to' means it is not necessary: You don't have to come if you're busy.

wrongReasons.has: After 'don't' we use the base form 'have'.

questions.text: You don't ___ to bring food. We'll have lots at the party.

questions.explanation: Modal verbs are followed by the base form without 'to': You should drink more water.

wrongReasons.to go: 'should' is followed by the base form without 'to'.
wrongReasons.going: After 'should' we use the base form, not the -ing form.

questions.text: You look tired. You should ___ to bed early tonight.

questions.explanation: Use 'could' for ability in the past: She could read when she was four.

wrongReasons.can: 'when I was five' is in the past, so use 'could'.
wrongReasons.must: 'must' is for obligation, not past ability.

questions.text: I ___ swim when I was five, but now I'm not very good.

questions.explanation: Use 'might' or 'may' for things that are possible in the future: It might snow tonight.

wrongReasons.must: 'must' shows certainty or obligation, not possibility.
wrongReasons.can: 'can' is not used for a possible future event like this.

questions.text: Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later.

questions.explanation: 'Have to' expresses necessity. With he, she and it use 'has to': He has to get up early.
questions.text: She ___ to wear glasses for reading.

questions.explanation: Use 'Can/Could/May I...?' to ask for permission: Can I sit here?

wrongReasons.must: 'Must I' asks if it is necessary, not for permission or as an offer.
wrongReasons.do: 'Do I open' is not used to ask for permission.

questions.text: ___ I open the window? It's very hot in here.

questions.explanation: Use 'must not' or 'may not' for rules that forbid something: Visitors must not feed the animals.

wrongReasons.don't: 'don't not use' has two negatives and is wrong.
wrongReasons.have: 'have not use' is wrong; 'have' needs 'to' for obligation.

questions.text: Students ___ not use their phones during the test.

questions.explanation: 'Had to' is the past of 'must/have to': I had to work late yesterday.

wrongReasons.for: 'had for wait' is not correct; use 'had to'.

questions.text: We had ___ wait two hours at the airport.

questions.explanation: Use 'shouldn't' to give advice not to do something: You shouldn't stay up so late.

wrongReasons.don't have to: 'don't have to' means it is not necessary; here we give advice not to do it.
wrongReasons.should: The sentence gives a reason not to do it, so use the negative 'shouldn't'.

questions.text: You ___ eat so much chocolate. It's bad for your teeth.

questions.explanation: Modals are followed by the base form: You must be quiet in the library.

wrongReasons.to be: 'must' is followed by the base form without 'to'.
wrongReasons.being: After 'must' use the base form, not the -ing form.

questions.text: He must ___ more careful with his money.

questions.explanation: Use 'couldn't' for something you were not able to do in the past: I couldn't sleep last night.

wrongReasons.can't: 'yesterday' is in the past, so use 'couldn't'.
wrongReasons.mustn't: 'mustn't' means it is forbidden, not that she was unable.

questions.text: Lucy ___ come to the meeting yesterday because she was ill.

questions.explanation: Questions with 'have to': Do/Does + subject + have to + verb? Do I have to sign here?

wrongReasons.for: 'have for pay' is not correct; use 'have to'.

questions.text: Do we have ___ pay for the museum, or is it free?

questions.explanation: Use 'might', 'may' or 'could' when you are not sure: She might be at home.

wrongReasons.must: 'must' shows you are sure, but the speaker is not sure.
wrongReasons.should: 'should' is mainly for advice or expectation, not a guess like this.

questions.text: I'm not sure where Ben is. He ___ be in the library.

questions.explanation: Use 'must' or 'have to' for rules and obligations: You have to wear a seat belt.

wrongReasons.can: 'can' shows ability or permission, not a legal rule.
wrongReasons.should: 'should' is only advice; a law is an obligation.

questions.text: You ___ be 18 to vote in this country. That is the law.

questions.explanation: Use 'could' for past ability or permission: Years ago you could smoke on planes.

wrongReasons.can: 'in the past' needs the past form 'could'.
wrongReasons.may: 'may' is not used for past ability or permission.

questions.text: In the past, people ___ travel abroad without a passport.

questions.explanation: Use 'mustn't' or 'can't' for things that are not allowed: You mustn't run by the pool.

wrongReasons.don't have to: 'don't have to' means it is not necessary, but touching is not allowed.
wrongReasons.needn't: 'needn't' means there is no need, not that it is forbidden.

questions.text: Visitors ___ touch the paintings. Please keep a safe distance.

questions.explanation: 'Didn't have to' means it was not necessary in the past: We didn't have to wait long.

wrongReasons.had: After 'didn't' we use the base form 'have'.
wrongReasons.must: 'must' is not followed by 'to' and has no past form.

questions.text: Our teacher said we didn't ___ to finish the essay today.

questions.explanation: Use 'used to' + base verb for past situations that are not true now: I used to have a dog.

wrongReasons.use: In positive sentences the form is 'used to', not 'use to'.
wrongReasons.using: 'using to' is not correct; the form is 'used to'.

questions.text: When I was a child, I ___ to live in a small village.

questions.explanation: In questions with 'did', write 'use to': Did you use to play tennis?

wrongReasons.used: After 'did' we use 'use to', not 'used to'.
wrongReasons.using: After 'did' we need the base form 'use'.

questions.text: Did you ___ to have long hair?

questions.explanation: In negatives, use 'didn't use to' + verb: I didn't use to drink tea.

wrongReasons.uses: After 'didn't' we need the base form 'use'.

questions.text: My father didn't ___ to like vegetables, but now he loves them.

questions.explanation: 'There used to be' talks about something that existed in the past: There used to be a lake here.

wrongReasons.is: After 'used to' we need the base form 'be'.
wrongReasons.being: After 'used to' (past habit) we need the base form, not -ing.

questions.text: There used to ___ a cinema on this street, but it closed.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb for past habits: We used to walk to school.

wrongReasons.wrote: After 'used to' we need the base form, not the past simple.
wrongReasons.writing: 'used to writing' means 'be familiar with'; here we need the base form.

questions.text: People used to ___ letters, but now they send emails.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + verb shows a past habit that has stopped: She used to sing in a choir.

wrongReasons.was used: 'was used to' has a different meaning (be familiar with) and needs -ing.

questions.text: I ___ to play the piano, but I stopped when I was twelve.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes regular actions in the past: He used to cycle to the office.

wrongReasons.went: After 'used to' we need the base form, not the past simple.
wrongReasons.going: After 'used to' for past habits we need the base form.

questions.text: My grandparents used to ___ to work by bike every day.

questions.explanation: Use 'used to' for repeated actions in the past: They used to visit us every Sunday.

wrongReasons.use: In positive sentences write 'used to', not 'use to'.
wrongReasons.are used: 'are used to' is present and means 'be familiar with'.

questions.text: We ___ to go camping every summer when the kids were small.

questions.explanation: Questions: Did + subject + use to + verb? Where did you use to live?

wrongReasons.for: The structure is 'use to', not 'use for'.

questions.text: Where did you use ___ go on holiday as a child?

questions.explanation: 'Used to' describes a past situation that has changed: This building used to be a school.

wrongReasons.uses: 'uses to' is not correct English; the form is 'used to'.

questions.text: This shop ___ to sell books, but now it sells clothes.

questions.explanation: Negative questions with 'used to': Didn't you use to live here?

wrongReasons.using: After 'didn't' we need the base form 'use'.

questions.text: Didn't you ___ to work at the bank on King Street?

questions.explanation: 'Never used to' + base verb means something was not true in the past: I never used to eat fish.

wrongReasons.drank: After 'used to' we need the base form.
wrongReasons.drinking: After 'used to' for past habits we need the base form, not -ing.

questions.text: I never used to ___ coffee, but now I drink three cups a day.

questions.explanation: Negative form: didn't use to + verb. She didn't use to like cats.

wrongReasons.doesn't: 'used to' is about the past, so use 'didn't'.
wrongReasons.wasn't: 'wasn't use to' is not correct; use 'didn't use to'.

questions.text: Tom ___ use to be so quiet. He has changed a lot.

questions.explanation: 'Used to be' describes past states: The town used to be very quiet.

wrongReasons.was used: 'was used to' means 'was familiar with', which does not fit here.

questions.text: Life ___ to be much slower before the internet.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + be for past states: He used to be a doctor.

wrongReasons.been: After 'used to' we need the base form 'be'.
wrongReasons.is: After 'used to' we need the base form, not 'is'.

questions.text: Our town used to ___ famous for its cheese.

questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb for past habits: My aunt used to spend winters in Spain.

wrongReasons.lived: After 'used to' we need the base form, not the past simple.
wrongReasons.living: After 'used to' for past habits we need the base form.

questions.text: The old king used to ___ in this castle in the summer.

questions.explanation: 'Used to be' + adjective for a past state; 'afraid' is followed by 'of': I used to be afraid of dogs.

wrongReasons.about: 'afraid about' is not the usual phrase; use 'afraid of'.

questions.text: My brother used to be afraid ___ the dark, but now he isn't.

questions.explanation: 'Enjoy' is followed by the -ing form of a verb. Example: She enjoys reading.

wrongReasons.to walk: 'Enjoy' is never followed by 'to' + verb; use the -ing form.
wrongReasons.walk: After 'enjoy' the verb needs the -ing ending.

questions.text: My grandfather enjoys ___ (walk) in the park every morning.

questions.explanation: 'Decide' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: They decided to stay at home.

wrongReasons.taking: 'Decide' is not followed by the -ing form; use 'to' + verb.
wrongReasons.take: You need 'to' before the verb after 'decide'.

questions.text: We decided ___ (take) the train because the roads were icy.

questions.explanation: 'Would you mind' is followed by the -ing form. Example: Would you mind waiting a moment?

wrongReasons.close: After 'mind' the verb must end in -ing.

questions.text: Would you mind ___ (close) the window? It's cold in here.

questions.explanation: 'Hope' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: I hope to see you soon.

wrongReasons.finishing: 'Hope' is not followed by the -ing form.

questions.text: The scientist hopes ___ (finish) her report before Friday.

questions.explanation: After a preposition like 'at', 'in' or 'of', use the -ing form. Example: He is good at singing.

wrongReasons.draw: After the preposition 'at' the verb must take -ing.
wrongReasons.to draw: 'Good at' is followed by -ing, not 'to' + verb.

questions.text: Lucy is very good at ___ (draw) animals.

questions.explanation: 'Promise' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: She promised to help me.
questions.text: He promised ___ (call) his mother when he arrived in Rome.

questions.explanation: 'Think of' ends with a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing. Example: We're thinking of moving.

wrongReasons.to join: 'Of' is a preposition, so it cannot be followed by 'to' + verb.
wrongReasons.join: After 'of' the verb needs the -ing form.

questions.text: I'm thinking of ___ (join) a photography club.

questions.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by the -ing form. Example: He suggested going for a walk.
questions.text: Our manager suggested ___ (have) the meeting online.

questions.explanation: 'Finish' is followed by the -ing form. Example: I finished cooking at seven.

wrongReasons.paint: After 'finish' the verb must end in -ing.

questions.text: Have you finished ___ (paint) the kitchen yet?

questions.explanation: 'Afford' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: We can't afford to travel this summer.
questions.text: She can't afford ___ (buy) a new car this year.

questions.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing. Example: I'm looking forward to meeting you.

wrongReasons.see: Here 'to' is a preposition, not part of the infinitive, so use -ing.
wrongReasons.seen: 'Seen' is a past participle; after a preposition use -ing.

questions.text: The children are looking forward to ___ (see) the dolphins.

questions.explanation: 'Refuse' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: He refused to pay.

wrongReasons.answering: 'Refuse' is not followed by the -ing form.
wrongReasons.answer: You need 'to' before the verb after 'refuse'.

questions.text: The lawyer refused ___ (answer) any more questions.

questions.explanation: 'Feel like' is followed by the -ing form. Example: I feel like going out.

wrongReasons.cook: 'Like' here is a preposition, so the verb needs -ing.

questions.text: I don't feel like ___ (cook) tonight. Let's order a pizza.

questions.explanation: 'Manage' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: She managed to open the door.
questions.text: They managed ___ (repair) the old bridge in just two weeks.

questions.explanation: 'Stop' + -ing means you end an activity. Example: Stop shouting, please.

wrongReasons.to talk: 'Stop to talk' means to stop doing something else in order to talk, which is not the meaning here.
wrongReasons.talk: After 'stop' the activity you end takes the -ing form.

questions.text: Please stop ___ (talk) during the film. I can't hear anything.

questions.explanation: After 'interested in' use the -ing form. Example: Are you interested in cooking?

wrongReasons.learn: 'In' is a preposition, so the verb needs -ing.
wrongReasons.to learn: 'Interested in' cannot be followed by 'to' + verb.

questions.text: My brother is interested in ___ (learn) Japanese.

questions.explanation: 'Agree' is followed by 'to' + base verb. Example: They agreed to share the cost.

wrongReasons.meet: You need 'to' before the verb after 'agree'.

questions.text: We agreed ___ (meet) outside the museum at ten.

questions.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by the -ing form. Example: I avoid eating late at night.

wrongReasons.drive: After 'avoid' the verb must end in -ing.

questions.text: Tom avoids ___ (drive) in the city centre at rush hour.

questions.explanation: Use 'be going to' for predictions based on what we can see now. Example: Look, he's going to fall!

wrongReasons.go: The structure is 'be going to', so you need the -ing form 'going'.
wrongReasons.will: 'Will' cannot follow 'it's' and is not followed by 'to'.

questions.text: Look at those dark clouds. It's ___ to rain.

questions.explanation: Use 'will' for a decision or offer made at the moment of speaking. Example: It's heavy? I'll carry it.

wrongReasons.am lending: The present continuous is for plans made before; this offer is decided now.
wrongReasons.lend: The present simple does not express an offer about the future here; use 'will'.

questions.text: Oh no, I've left my wallet at home! - Don't worry, I ___ (lend) you some money.

questions.explanation: Use the present continuous (be + -ing) to ask about future plans. Example: What are you doing tomorrow?

wrongReasons.do: 'Do' cannot be followed by an -ing verb like 'doing' here; you need 'are'.
wrongReasons.will: 'Will' is followed by a base verb, not 'doing'.

questions.text: What ___ you doing on Saturday night? - I'm meeting some friends.

questions.explanation: Use 'be going to' for a decision you have already made. Example: I'm going to learn French.

wrongReasons.be: The verb 'be' must agree with 'I', so it is 'am'.

questions.text: I've decided. I ___ going to study medicine at university.

questions.explanation: The structure is 'be going to' + base verb. Example: She's going to win.

wrongReasons.for: 'Going for' is not used before a verb.
wrongReasons.fall: 'Going' must be followed by 'to' before the verb.

questions.text: Watch out! That tree is going ___ fall on the car!

questions.explanation: In questions with 'going to', put 'is/are/am' before the subject. Example: When is he going to leave?

wrongReasons.are: 'Your sister' is singular, so the verb is 'is'.
wrongReasons.does: 'Going to' questions use the verb 'be', not 'do'.

questions.text: Where ___ your sister going to stay in London? - With her friend Anna.

questions.explanation: Use the present continuous for fixed future arrangements. Example: We are moving house in May.

wrongReasons.is: 'Kate and Ben' are two people, so you need 'are'.
wrongReasons.will: 'Will' is followed by a base verb, not 'getting'.

questions.text: Kate and Ben ___ getting married next spring. The invitations have already been sent.

questions.explanation: Use 'will' or 'won't' for promises. Example: I won't be late, I promise.

wrongReasons.don't: Promises about the future use 'won't', not the present simple.
wrongReasons.not: 'Not' alone cannot make a verb negative; you need 'will not' or 'won't'.

questions.text: I promise I ___ tell anyone your secret.

questions.explanation: Questions with 'be going to' follow the pattern 'Are you going to + verb?'. Example: Are you going to call her?

wrongReasons.go: After 'are you' you need the -ing form 'going'.
wrongReasons.want: 'Are you want' is not correct; 'want' does not take 'are'.

questions.text: Are you ___ to watch the match tonight?

questions.explanation: Negative 'going to': 'I'm not going to' + base verb. Example: I'm not going to buy it.

wrongReasons.watch: 'Going' must be followed by 'to' before the verb.
wrongReasons.watching: After 'going' you need 'to' + base verb, not -ing.

questions.text: I'm not going ___ that film. I heard it's boring.

questions.explanation: The negative of 'be going to' is 'is not / isn't going to'. Example: She isn't going to come.

wrongReasons.doesn't: 'Going to' uses the verb 'be' in the negative, not 'do'.
wrongReasons.won't: 'Won't' is not used together with 'going to'.

questions.text: He ___ going to buy a new laptop. His old one works fine.

questions.explanation: For future plans, use the present continuous, 'going to' or 'will'. Example: He isn't coming to dinner tonight.

wrongReasons.doesn't come: The present simple is not used for a personal plan like this one.
wrongReasons.not come: A negative verb needs an auxiliary like 'isn't' or 'won't'.

questions.text: She ___ (not / come) to the party tomorrow. She has to work.

questions.explanation: Use the present simple for timetables and schedules. Example: The train leaves at six.

wrongReasons.finish: 'The film' is singular, so the present simple needs -es.
wrongReasons.is finish: 'Is' cannot be followed by the base verb 'finish'.

questions.text: The film starts at 8:00 and ___ (finish) at 10:30.

questions.explanation: Use 'I think I'll...' for a decision made now. Example: I think I'll have the soup.

wrongReasons.go: The present simple does not express this decision about tonight.
wrongReasons.am go: 'Am' cannot be followed directly by the base verb.

questions.text: I'm so tired. I think I ___ (go) to bed early tonight.

questions.explanation: Use 'will' after 'I think / I don't think' for predictions. Example: I don't think it will rain.

wrongReasons.is being: 'Is being' describes behaviour now, not a prediction.
wrongReasons.be: The base verb alone cannot follow 'the exam'; you need 'will be'.

questions.text: I don't think the exam ___ (be) very difficult.

questions.explanation: Use the present continuous for arrangements that are already booked. Example: I'm seeing the dentist on Monday.

wrongReasons.fly: The present simple is used for timetables, not for personal arrangements.
wrongReasons.flew: 'Flew' is the past; the trip is on Friday, in the future.

questions.text: We ___ (fly) to Lisbon on Friday. We booked the tickets last month.

questions.explanation: Use 'will' for an offer or decision made at the moment of speaking. Example: Someone's at the door. I'll go.

wrongReasons.am answering: The present continuous is for plans made earlier, not a quick decision now.
wrongReasons.answer: The present simple does not make an offer; use 'will'.

questions.text: The phone is ringing. - Don't move, I ___ (answer) it.

questions.explanation: Use 'will' or 'going to' for predictions about the future. Example: It will be cold tonight.

wrongReasons.is being: 'Is being' is not used for weather predictions.
wrongReasons.be: 'It be' is not correct; you need 'will be'.

questions.text: The weather forecast says it ___ (be) sunny tomorrow.

questions.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' for people in relative clauses. Example: The man who called you is my uncle.

wrongReasons.which: 'Which' is for things and animals, not people.

questions.text: The woman ___ runs the bakery on our street is from Portugal.

questions.explanation: Use 'where' for places when the clause has its own subject. Example: That's the café where we met.

wrongReasons.which: 'Which' would need 'in' or 'at' at the end: 'which we stayed in'.

questions.text: This is the hotel ___ we stayed last summer.

questions.explanation: Use 'which' or 'that' for things. Example: The book that you lent me is great.

wrongReasons.who: 'Who' is used for people, not objects.
wrongReasons.where: 'Where' is for places, not things like a phone.

questions.text: The phone ___ I bought last week has stopped working.

questions.explanation: Use 'whose' to show possession (his, her, their). Example: That's the girl whose cat is lost.

wrongReasons.who's: 'Who's' means 'who is', which does not fit before 'father is'.
wrongReasons.who: 'Who' does not show possession; you need 'whose'.

questions.text: I have a friend ___ father is a famous chef.

questions.explanation: Use 'where' after a place noun. Example: This is the town where I was born.

wrongReasons.that: 'That' would need a preposition at the end ('met in'); use 'where'.
wrongReasons.which: 'Which' alone does not fit; you would need 'in which'.

questions.text: Paris is the city ___ my parents first met.

questions.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' for people. Example: The players who won got a medal.

wrongReasons.whose: 'Whose' shows possession and needs a noun after it.

questions.text: The students ___ passed the exam received a certificate.

questions.explanation: Use 'that' or 'which' for things. Example: I love the film that won the prize.

wrongReasons.who: A song is a thing, so 'who' is wrong.
wrongReasons.what: 'What' cannot follow a noun like 'the song'.

questions.text: Do you remember the song ___ was playing when we met?

questions.explanation: In a clause between commas (extra information), use 'which' for things, never 'that'. Example: My car, which is red, is old.

wrongReasons.that: 'That' is not used after a comma to add extra information.
wrongReasons.who: A museum is a thing, not a person.

questions.text: The museum, ___ opened in 1890, is the oldest in the country.

questions.explanation: In a clause between commas, use 'who' for people. Example: My sister, who lives in Leeds, is a teacher.

wrongReasons.that: 'That' cannot be used after a comma.
wrongReasons.which: 'Which' is for things, but an uncle is a person.

questions.text: My uncle, ___ is a pilot, has visited over fifty countries.

questions.explanation: Use 'where' for places. Example: This is the park where we play tennis.

wrongReasons.which: 'Which' would need 'from' at the end of the clause.
wrongReasons.who: A shop is a place, so 'who' does not fit.

questions.text: That's the shop ___ I buy my vegetables.

questions.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' for people. Example: The teacher who I like most is Mr Brown.

wrongReasons.which: 'Which' is not used for people like a doctor.
wrongReasons.whose: 'Whose' needs a noun after it to show possession.

questions.text: The doctor ___ I saw yesterday was very kind.

questions.explanation: Use 'that' or 'which' for things. Example: Is this the key that opens the door?

wrongReasons.what: 'What' cannot come after a noun like 'the bag'.

questions.text: Is this the bag ___ you lost at the airport?

questions.explanation: Use 'where' to talk about what happens in a place. Example: It's a city where people cycle a lot.

wrongReasons.which: 'Which' alone does not fit because the clause already has a subject and object.
wrongReasons.who: 'Who' refers to people, but here it follows 'village', a place.

questions.text: We visited a village ___ people still make bread in the old way.

questions.explanation: Use 'whose' + noun to show that something belongs to someone. Example: She's the writer whose books I love.

wrongReasons.who: 'Who films' is not correct; you need the possessive 'whose'.
wrongReasons.which: 'Which' is for things and does not show possession here.

questions.text: He's the actor ___ films have won many prizes.

questions.explanation: Use 'that' or 'which' for things and vehicles. Example: The train that goes to York is late.

wrongReasons.who: A bus is a thing, so 'who' is wrong.

questions.text: The bus ___ goes to the airport leaves every twenty minutes.

questions.explanation: Use 'whose' to mean 'her/his' in a relative clause. Example: Tom, whose dog is ill, is at the vet.

wrongReasons.who: 'Who brother' is wrong; to show possession use 'whose'.
wrongReasons.that: 'That' cannot follow a comma and does not show possession.

questions.text: Anna, ___ brother plays in a band, wants to be a singer too.

questions.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that' for people. Example: I know someone who speaks five languages.

wrongReasons.whose: 'Whose' must be followed by a noun.

questions.text: I don't like people ___ talk loudly on the phone in the cinema.

questions.explanation: Use 'that' or 'which' for things. Example: The car that we rented was new.

wrongReasons.who: A computer is not a person, so 'who' is wrong.
wrongReasons.what: 'What' is not used after a noun like 'the computer'.

questions.text: The computer ___ we use at work is very slow.

questions.explanation: 'Turn up' means make louder; 'turn down' means make quieter. Example: Turn up the radio, please.

wrongReasons.down: 'Turn down' makes the sound quieter, but the speaker can't hear.
wrongReasons.on: You turn on a machine, not the volume.

questions.text: Could you turn ___ the volume a little? I can't hear the news.

questions.explanation: 'Look for' means try to find something. Example: She's looking for her glasses.

wrongReasons.after: 'Look after' means take care of someone or something.
wrongReasons.at: 'Look at' means direct your eyes towards something you can already see.

questions.text: I'm looking ___ my keys. Have you seen them?

questions.explanation: 'Fill in' or 'fill out' means write the information a form asks for. Example: Fill in your name here.

wrongReasons.on: 'Fill on' is not a phrasal verb in English.
wrongReasons.up: 'Fill up' means make a container full, like a glass or a car.

questions.text: Please fill ___ this form and give it to the receptionist.

questions.explanation: 'Look after' means take care of someone. Example: Can you look after my cat this weekend?

wrongReasons.for: 'Look for' means search for, not take care of.
wrongReasons.at: 'Look at' means watch or see, not take care of.

questions.text: My grandmother looked ___ me when my parents were at work.

questions.explanation: 'Run out of' means have no more of something. Example: We've run out of coffee.

wrongReasons.off: 'Run off' means leave quickly; it is not used with 'of milk'.
wrongReasons.away: 'Run away' means escape from a place.

questions.text: We ran ___ of milk, so I went to the shop.

questions.explanation: 'Take off' means leave the ground (for planes). Example: Our flight takes off at noon.

wrongReasons.out: 'Take out' means remove something from a place.
wrongReasons.up: 'Take up' means start a new hobby.

questions.text: The plane took ___ two hours late because of the fog.

questions.explanation: 'Give up' means stop doing something. Example: He gave up smoking last year.

wrongReasons.out: 'Give out' means hand things to people.
wrongReasons.off: 'Give off' means send out a smell or heat.

questions.text: I gave ___ eating chocolate for a month. It was really hard!

questions.explanation: You 'get on' and 'get off' buses, trains and planes. Example: Get off at the next stop.

wrongReasons.out: 'Get out of' is used for cars and taxis, and it needs 'of'.
wrongReasons.down: 'Get down' means move to a lower position; it is not used with 'the bus'.

questions.text: He got ___ the bus at the wrong stop and had to walk home.

questions.explanation: 'Pick someone up' means collect them in a car. Example: I'll pick you up after school.

wrongReasons.off: 'Pick off' is not the meaning of collecting someone.

questions.text: Can you pick me ___ from the station at six?

questions.explanation: 'Switch off' means stop a machine or light working. Example: Switch off your phone in the cinema.

wrongReasons.on: 'Switch on' means start the lights, but you are leaving.
wrongReasons.out: We say 'put out' a fire, but not 'switch out' a light.

questions.text: Don't forget to switch ___ the lights when you leave the office.

questions.explanation: 'Look forward to' means feel happy about something in the future. Example: We look forward to the holidays.

wrongReasons.at: 'Look forward at' is not used in English.

questions.text: I'm really looking forward ___ your visit next month.

questions.explanation: 'Find out' means discover information. Example: I found out his name.

wrongReasons.up: 'Find up' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.about: 'Find about' is wrong; you can say 'find out about'.

questions.text: She found ___ the truth from a friend.

questions.explanation: 'Set off' or 'set out' means start a journey. Example: We set off at dawn.

wrongReasons.up: 'Set up' means start a business or prepare equipment.
wrongReasons.on: 'Set on' does not mean start a journey.

questions.text: We need to set ___ early tomorrow to avoid the traffic.

questions.explanation: 'Grow up' means change from a child into an adult. Example: I grew up in a small town.

wrongReasons.out: 'Grow out of' means become too big for clothes.
wrongReasons.in: 'Grow in' is not a phrasal verb with this meaning.

questions.text: The children grew ___ on a farm in Wales.

questions.explanation: 'Hold on' means wait for a short time. Example: Hold on, I'm coming.

wrongReasons.up: 'Hold up' means delay someone or something.
wrongReasons.off: 'Hold off' means delay doing something, not wait a moment on the phone.

questions.text: Can you hold ___ a minute? I'll get a pen.

questions.explanation: 'Try on' means put on clothes to see if they fit. Example: Can I try on these shoes?

wrongReasons.in: 'Try in' is not a phrasal verb.
wrongReasons.up: 'Try up' does not exist in English.

questions.text: Why don't you try ___ the jacket before you buy it?

questions.explanation: 'Break down' means stop working (for machines and cars). Example: The bus broke down on the way.

wrongReasons.out: 'Break out' means start suddenly, like a fire or war.

questions.text: Our car broke ___ on the motorway, so we called a mechanic.

questions.explanation: 'Put out' means stop something burning. Example: They put out the fire quickly.

wrongReasons.off: 'Put off' means delay something until later.
wrongReasons.down: 'Put down' means place something on a surface.

questions.text: Could you put ___ your cigarette, please? Smoking isn't allowed here.

questions.explanation: Use 'because' to give a reason. Example: She was happy because she passed the test.

wrongReasons.so: 'So' introduces a result, not a reason.
wrongReasons.although: 'Although' shows a contrast, but having a cold is a reason for staying at home.

questions.text: I stayed at home ___ I had a bad cold.

questions.explanation: Use 'so' to introduce a result. Example: I was hungry, so I made a sandwich.

wrongReasons.because: 'Because' gives a reason, but taking a taxi is the result.
wrongReasons.however: 'However' shows a contrast and is not used to join two clauses with a comma.

questions.text: It was raining, ___ we took a taxi.

questions.explanation: Use 'although' to join two ideas that contrast. Example: Although it was cold, we went swimming.

wrongReasons.because: 'Because' gives a reason, but here the two ideas contrast.
wrongReasons.however: 'However' cannot join two clauses like this.

questions.text: ___ the hotel was expensive, we didn't enjoy our stay.

questions.explanation: 'However' starts a new sentence and shows contrast; put a comma after it. Example: It was hard. However, I finished it.

wrongReasons.although: 'Although' must join two clauses in one sentence; it cannot stand alone with a comma.
wrongReasons.but: 'But' is not followed by a comma at the start of a sentence like this.

questions.text: The film was very long. ___, it was never boring.

questions.explanation: Use 'but' to join two contrasting ideas. Example: He is rich, but he is not happy.

wrongReasons.so: 'So' shows a result, but failing is not a result of studying hard.
wrongReasons.because: 'Because' gives a reason, which does not fit here.

questions.text: She studied hard, ___ she failed the driving test.

questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing form. Example: Despite the rain, we played football.

wrongReasons.although: 'Although' needs a full clause after it, not just a noun.
wrongReasons.however: 'However' cannot go before a noun like this.

questions.text: We went to the beach ___ the cold weather.

questions.explanation: Use 'but' or 'while' to compare two different things. Example: I like tea, but my wife prefers coffee.

wrongReasons.so: 'So' introduces a result, not a difference.
wrongReasons.because: 'Because' gives a reason, but here two people are compared.

questions.text: My brother likes sports, ___ I prefer reading.

questions.explanation: Use 'because' before a reason. Example: We left early because it was late.

wrongReasons.so: 'So' would make the alarm the result, but it is the reason.

questions.text: He was late for work ___ his alarm didn't ring.

questions.explanation: Use 'so' to show what happened as a result. Example: The bus didn't come, so we walked.

wrongReasons.because: 'Because' introduces a reason, but going to a café is the result.
wrongReasons.although: 'Although' shows contrast, which does not fit here.

questions.text: The museum was closed, ___ we went to a café instead.

questions.explanation: 'However' shows contrast with the sentence before. Example: I hate running. However, I do it every day.

wrongReasons.although: 'Although' must be followed by a clause in the same sentence, not a comma.
wrongReasons.so: 'So' shows a result, but this is a contrast.

questions.text: I don't usually eat meat. ___, I sometimes have chicken at my grandmother's house.

questions.explanation: 'Unless' means 'if not'. Example: You won't pass unless you study.

wrongReasons.if: 'If' gives the opposite meaning: you can't enter if you're an adult.
wrongReasons.because: 'Because' gives a reason, which makes no sense here.

questions.text: You can't enter the club ___ you're over eighteen.

questions.explanation: Use 'although' + clause to show contrast. Example: Although he was ill, he went to work.

wrongReasons.despite: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or -ing, not a full clause like 'I was tired'.
wrongReasons.so: 'So' cannot start a sentence to show contrast.

questions.text: ___ I was tired, I finished the report before midnight.

questions.explanation: 'Because of' is followed by a noun. Example: We stayed in because of the rain.

wrongReasons.because: 'Because' must be followed by a clause with a verb, not just a noun.
wrongReasons.so: 'So' introduces a result, not a cause.

questions.text: The flight was cancelled ___ the storm.

questions.explanation: Use 'then' or 'next' to show the order of steps. Example: First, wash the vegetables. Then, cut them.

wrongReasons.before: 'Before' needs a noun or clause after it, and it does not fit the order of steps.
wrongReasons.so: 'So' shows a result, not the next step.

questions.text: First, mix the flour and the sugar. ___, add the eggs.

questions.explanation: 'Also' adds information and goes before the main verb. Example: He plays the guitar. He also sings.

wrongReasons.too: 'Too' goes at the end of the sentence, not before the verb.

questions.text: Maria speaks Spanish and French. She ___ speaks a little Chinese.

questions.explanation: Use 'or' / 'otherwise' to show what will happen if something is not done. Example: Hurry, or you'll miss the bus.

wrongReasons.so: 'So' would mean the call makes me worry, which is the opposite.
wrongReasons.and: 'And' does not show what happens if you don't call.

questions.text: Call me when you arrive, ___ I'll worry about you.

questions.explanation: Use 'while' or 'when' + clause for something happening at the same time. Example: I fell while I was running.

wrongReasons.during: 'During' is followed by a noun, not a clause.
wrongReasons.so: 'So' shows a result, not the time something happened.

questions.text: I hurt my knee ___ I was playing football.

questions.explanation: We say 'do someone a favour'. Example: Could you do me a favour?

wrongReasons.give: 'Give a favour' is not a natural English expression.

questions.text: Can you ___ me a favour and post this letter?

questions.explanation: We say 'make an appointment' or 'book an appointment'. Example: I made an appointment for Monday.

wrongReasons.take: In English we don't usually say 'take an appointment'.

questions.text: I need to ___ an appointment with the dentist.

questions.explanation: We say 'make progress'. Example: She is making good progress at school.

wrongReasons.did: 'Did' is the past simple; after 'has' you need a past participle, and the verb is 'make'.

questions.text: My brother has ___ a lot of progress with his English this year.

questions.explanation: We say 'do your homework'. Example: I do my homework after school.

wrongReasons.write: We don't usually say 'write your homework'; the common verb is 'do'.

questions.text: Don't forget to ___ your homework before dinner.

questions.explanation: 'Crowded' means full of people. Example: The beach was crowded in August.

wrongReasons.empty: 'Empty' means with no people, so you could sit down.
wrongReasons.crowd: 'Crowd' is a noun; you need the adjective 'crowded'.

questions.text: The train was very ___, so we had to stand all the way.

questions.explanation: A dentist looks after your teeth. Example: I see the dentist twice a year.

wrongReasons.chemist: A chemist sells medicine, but does not fix teeth.
wrongReasons.hairdresser: A hairdresser cuts hair and cannot help with a toothache.

questions.text: I went to the ___ because I had a terrible toothache.

questions.explanation: You 'lend' something to someone; you 'borrow' something from someone. Example: Can you lend me five pounds?

wrongReasons.borrow: 'Borrow' means take from someone; with 'me' as the receiver you need 'lend'.
wrongReasons.give: 'Give' means it becomes mine, but the speaker will return it.

questions.text: Could you ___ me your pen for a moment? I'll give it back.

questions.explanation: A cancelled flight does not happen at all. Example: The match was cancelled because of rain.

wrongReasons.cancel: After 'was' you need the past participle 'cancelled'.
wrongReasons.closed: A flight is not 'closed'; shops and doors are closed.

questions.text: Our flight was ___ because of the snow, so we stayed another night in the hotel.

questions.explanation: You 'withdraw' or 'get' money from a cash machine. Example: I withdrew fifty euros.

wrongReasons.borrow: You borrow money from a person or bank, not from a cash machine.
wrongReasons.lend: 'Lend' means give money to someone for a short time.

questions.text: I'd like to ___ some money from the cash machine.

questions.explanation: We say 'take / catch the bus'. Example: I take the bus to school.

wrongReasons.makes: 'Make the bus' is not used for travelling.

questions.text: She ___ the bus every morning to get to work.

questions.explanation: We say 'pay attention'. Example: Pay attention to the teacher.

wrongReasons.give: 'Attention' goes with 'pay', not 'give', in this phrase.

questions.text: Please ___ attention. This information is important.

questions.explanation: We say 'take / get a taxi'. Example: Let's take a taxi to the airport.

wrongReasons.drive: You drive a car yourself; a taxi driver drives the taxi for you.
wrongReasons.go: 'Go a taxi' is wrong; you can say 'go by taxi'.

questions.text: It's very late. I'm going to ___ a taxi home.

questions.explanation: A pilot is the person who flies a plane. Example: The pilot spoke to the passengers.

wrongReasons.flight attendant: A flight attendant looks after the passengers, but does not fly the plane.
wrongReasons.driver: A driver drives cars, buses or trains, not planes.

questions.text: She works as a ___. She flies planes for a big airline.

questions.explanation: 'Expensive' is the opposite of 'cheap'. Example: Hotels in the centre are expensive.

wrongReasons.rich: 'Rich' describes people with a lot of money, not prices.
wrongReasons.cheaper: 'Cheaper' is wrong because that watch costs a lot.

questions.text: This watch was cheap, but that one costs a lot. It's really ___.

questions.explanation: 'Postpone' or 'put off' means move something to a later time. Example: They postponed the match.

wrongReasons.cancel: 'Cancel' means it will not happen at all, but 'until next week' shows it will happen later.
wrongReasons.postponed: After 'had to' you need the base verb, not the past form.

questions.text: We had to ___ the meeting until next week because the boss was ill.

questions.explanation: 'Break' is irregular: break - broke - broken. Example: He broke his leg skiing.

wrongReasons.breaked: 'Break' is irregular; the past simple is 'broke', not 'breaked'.
wrongReasons.broken: 'Broken' is the past participle; the past simple is 'broke'.

questions.text: My cousin ___ her wrist when she fell off her bike last week.

questions.explanation: We say 'set / lay the table' (put out plates, knives and forks). Example: Can you set the table for four?

wrongReasons.make: You 'make' a bed, but you 'set' a table.
wrongReasons.do: 'Do the table' is not a natural English expression.

questions.text: Could you ___ the table, please? Dinner is almost ready.
